editorialStandard: Long-form sports journalism grounded in canonical weekly team results, verified playoff brackets, trades when available, and, for 2020–2025, the exact championship and semifinal player starter points archived in championship_player_boxscores_2020_2025_v1.json. 2016–2019 player MVPs and unsupported transactions are intentionally not invented. Early ESPN final scores in 2016 and 2017 are two-week aggregates; 2016–2018 scoring differs from 2019 and later.

seasons.title: The First Name on the Trophy
seasons.dek: A 1–3 start, two old rivals and a third seed that wrote the league’s first championship ending.

sections.heading: The season nobody would have scripted
sections.text: The Fellas' first champion was 1–3 after four weeks. Before anyone could build a dynasty, Thommy had to rescue an inaugural season that looked nothing like a coronation. Koble and Evans beat him early; Halderman, not Thommy, eventually set the regular-season pace at 8–4–1. The eventual champion was 7–5–1, third in a four-team championship bracket. There was no dominant wire-to-wire march, and no way to mistake this team for the favorite by looking only at the standings. That distinction matters: the first trophy went to someone who first had to prove he belonged in the postseason conversation. The older ESPN record establishes team scores and results, but it does not contain the individual starter box scores or a verified ledger of 2016 roster acquisitions. Naming a star player, a miracle trade or a championship-game MVP from this evidence would be fiction.

sections.heading: Four wins and the thinnest margins
sections.text: What happened between that 1–3 beginning and the first championship bracket is where the season began to turn. Thommy won four straight from Weeks 5 through 8, a stretch that took him past Stew, Halderman, Stover and Schermerhorn. In Week 6 he beat the eventual top seed Halderman 101–92. In Week 12, a 103–99 victory over Stew showed exactly how narrow the path could become: four points separated a crucial win from another setback. Evans still administered a 153–107 loss in Week 9, and Stilly beat Thommy in Week 11. Even the final regular-season meeting with Halderman finished level, 121–121. That tie was an almost cinematic preview of the game that would matter most. The season supplied no clean upward line; it supplied enough wins at the right moments to enter a four-team field.

sections.heading: First, a nemesis; then, the favorite
sections.text: The semifinal was an opportunity for an immediate correction. Evans had beaten Thommy twice during the regular season. Across the two-week semifinal, the result reversed: Thommy 227, Evans 153, a 74-point escape from the opponent who had seemed to know his weaknesses. The final was against Halderman, the regular-season leader and the opponent from the 121–121 Week 13 tie. Here the format matters. Those early ESPN championship scores were two-week aggregates, not single-Sunday totals. Thommy won 223–175, a 48-point margin over the strongest regular-season résumé. He did not merely avoid an upset against a lesser seed; he eliminated the manager who had topped the league and the one who had beaten him twice. The bracket, rather than reputation, determined the inaugural champion.

sections.heading: Why the first ring endures
sections.text: It is tempting to write the first Fellas title as destiny because later seasons made Thommy a dynasty. In 2016, nothing about the opening month looked inevitable. His defining contribution was navigating the middle of the season and then changing the outcome of two familiar matchups when elimination arrived. The verified MVP of this story is the postseason turnaround itself; the available ESPN files cannot responsibly identify the players who carried those particular two-week lineups. That is a limitation worth preserving, not papering over with a familiar NFL name. The result was larger than a single score. The league’s first championship established its enduring argument: regular-season leaders earn an advantage, but a title belongs to the manager who wins the games on the bracket. The first engraving was not reserved for the manager with the best record. It went to someone who had already learned how much a standings table can conceal. For every later Fellas champion, that first December supplied the precedent: the trophy measures what happened when the season could no longer offer a second chance.

insideTheRun.heading: The matchup that made the first champion
paragraphs: The final carried a wonderfully strange piece of symmetry. Halderman had set the regular-season pace at 8–4–1; Thommy entered the four-team bracket at 7–5–1. Their final regular-season meeting finished 121–121. When the championship brought them together again, there was no tie to hide behind: over two scoring weeks, Thommy won 223–175. The decisive difference wasn't a single documented play. It was a third seed outscoring the league leader by 48 in the only meeting that awarded a trophy.

The road also ran through Evans, who had beaten Thommy twice before December. The 227–153 semifinal reversal makes this title more than a lucky draw. Thommy had to overturn two established matchup narratives in succession. The recovered ESPN archive tells us the opponents and the margins, not which NFL players supplied every point. The defining protagonists we can name with certainty are the managers on the bracket.

seasons.title: The Champion Becomes the Standard
seasons.dek: The first repeat winner survived a 16-point semifinal and beat the opponent who had humbled him in October.

sections.heading: A target on the champion’s back
sections.text: The first Fellas title had made Thommy a champion. The second would make everyone else chase him. He entered 2017 as the only manager who knew what winning the league felt like—but defending the trophy required a different season entirely. In 2016 the title had come from the No. 3 seed; in 2017 he won his first four games and eventually finished 8–4, earning the No. 1 seed. The undefeated start included a 114–107 victory over Evans in Week 4, a seven-point margin that reminded everyone how quickly an apparently secure win could turn. The record was not spotless. Stover, Stilly and Schermerhorn handed Thommy losses in the middle of the year. In Week 7 Schermerhorn beat him 124–90, a 34-point warning from the manager he would eventually see again on the season’s final stage.

sections.heading: The response that secured the bracket
sections.text: The first seed had to be earned in the regular season; a second ring would still have to be earned in the bracket. Thommy put together evidence rather than relying on history. Week 9 brought a 148–63 victory over Birch, an 85-point separation that was one of the clearest expressions of the roster’s scoring ceiling. Late wins over Koble and Stew mattered in another way. The Koble contest ended 99–93, just six points apart; the regular-season finale against Stew ended with 137 for Thommy. Those games helped turn a lurching middle of the year into the league’s top playoff seed. We can track those swings from the archived ESPN matchup ledger. We cannot attribute them to named starters or transactions without original roster-level receipts, so the analysis here rests on what the scoreboard actually preserves.

sections.heading: The Evans escape and Schermerhorn reversal
sections.text: The first elimination game was no coronation. Evans, a familiar postseason opponent, made the two-week semifinal a 233–217 contest. Sixteen points across an entire two-week aggregate is a narrow cushion for a team carrying the No. 1 seed. Thommy held it and reached a second consecutive final. Waiting there was Schermerhorn, who had beaten him comfortably in Week 7. The rematch reversed the direction of the season series. Thommy scored 241 over the two-week championship, Schermerhorn 212. A 29-point margin was decisive, but it was earned against the one opponent who had exposed the champion most sharply in the regular season. The title run was built on two corrections: survive Evans, then solve Schermerhorn.

sections.heading: From an upset winner to a standard
sections.text: The first title had shown Thommy could win from the underdog’s side of the bracket. The second proved he could defend a top seed and withstand the expectation that came with it. Those are different achievements. Two championships in two seasons did not arise from the same script: one was a rise from a 1–3 opening and a third seed; the next came from an 8–4 first-place finish and a semifinal that stayed uncomfortable until the end. The individual 2017 playoff player scoring is not preserved in the available record, so no name can honestly be singled out as a box-score MVP. The surviving evidence is still compelling. Thommy had become the first repeat champion, and every contender now had a clear measuring stick. This time there was nowhere to hide behind the underdog label. Thommy had the first seed, the first championship to defend and a field eager to make the inaugural winner a one-year story. The second ring turned an upset into a standard—and made the next season a test of whether anyone could stop the same name being engraved again.

insideTheRun.heading: Sixteen points between a repeat and a reset
paragraphs: The championship rematch with Schermerhorn makes sense only after the semifinal. Evans held Thommy to a 233–217 two-week aggregate, a gap of just 16 across an extended elimination series. One swing in that two-week total could have made a defending champion a footnote instead of a repeat winner. Then came Schermerhorn, the manager who had beaten Thommy 124–90 in Week 7. The title was not secured by avoiding that difficult opponent; it was secured by reversing the matchup at the moment of maximum pressure.

The final finished 241–212, another two-week aggregate rather than a one-week fantasy explosion. The contrast with 2016 is the heart of the feature: Thommy's first title came from the No. 3 seed; his second came from the top line of the bracket. The same champion proved he could survive both roles. The preserved scores support that argument, but without original individual ESPN starter totals they cannot establish a named player-of-the-game.

seasons.title: Three in a Row, by Inches
seasons.dek: Three elimination games, a 3.90-point escape and a final decided by 4.96: the narrowest route to a dynasty.

sections.heading: The defense of a dynasty looked fragile
sections.text: The third consecutive championship would be decided by inches: a 3.90-point playoff escape, then a final won by 4.96. Before that heart-stopping December, Thommy was already chasing a distinction no Fella had ever approached—three titles in the league's first three seasons. The regular season, though, was not a procession. He finished 7–6, while Tony led the field at 8–5. Birch had crushed him 141.84–83.08 in Week 2. Stilly won their Week 8 meeting by nearly 40. Mitch held him to 73.02 in a Week 13 loss. Yet there were hints of the close-game nerve that would soon decide everything. In Week 7, Thommy beat Stew 142.92–142.76, a victory by sixteen hundredths of a point. The archived game scores are precise, but the older ESPN lineups and transaction histories are not complete enough to identify the individual play or player that separated those teams.

sections.heading: One wrong turn and the three-peat vanishes
sections.text: Those near misses in the regular season became the governing theme of December. Thommy entered the six-team playoffs as the No. 4 seed. That meant no bye, and no room for the slow starts a reigning champion might have survived in earlier Decembers. Kuhl forced the opening round into a 96.54–92.64 knife-edge. A 3.90-point victory kept the dynasty alive; one additional ordinary scoring play in the opposite direction could have ended it. Tony, the regular-season leader, awaited in the semifinal. Thommy produced a 94.80–82.30 win, moving past the league’s best regular-season record by 12.50 points. The first two elimination games had now both been won, but neither score suggested the favorite was cruising. A title defense that began at 7–6 had become a test of whether a manager could get precisely enough production for three consecutive weeks.

sections.heading: Birch, a four-point final, and immortality
sections.text: The title game supplied the opponent who had embarrassed Thommy in September: Birch. This was a rematch with real stakes. The same team that had won their Week 2 matchup by 58.76 points was now standing between Thommy and a third consecutive championship. The result went the other way, by a fraction of that earlier margin. Thommy scored 111.58; Birch, 106.62. The difference was 4.96 points. Combined with the 3.90-point opener and 12.50-point semifinal, the entire three-game postseason route was won by an aggregate 21.36 points. Two elimination games had been decided by fewer than five. The third title did not arrive with a blowout. It arrived because each close score ended with Thommy just ahead.

sections.heading: The third ring means more because it almost wasn't
sections.text: Three championships in three Fellas seasons is an unmistakable dynasty marker. What makes 2018 worth a long-form account is not simply the number three. It is how often that third trophy could have slipped away. The team that had lost badly to Birch in Week 2, finished barely over .500 and opened the playoffs in a near tie with Kuhl still found its way into the final and survived there by 4.96. Later history can add famous names to the league’s story, but the preserved ESPN archive does not safely establish 2018 title-game player MVPs or consequential completed trades. The evidence that survives already makes the case: when the three-peat was most vulnerable, the scoreboard kept giving Thommy another week. Birch would take the trophy the next season. That fact makes the 2018 final feel even sharper in retrospect: the future champion had Thommy within 4.96 points and could not break the streak. The dynasty was not an uninterrupted procession of dominant scores. It was three consecutive Decembers in which nobody quite delivered the last blow.

insideTheRun.heading: A dynasty measured in decimal places
paragraphs: Consider the alternative history hiding inside the numbers. Kuhl lost the opening-round matchup 96.54–92.64; Birch lost the championship 111.58–106.62. The margins were 3.90 and 4.96. Those two games alone account for just 8.86 points of separation, despite deciding whether the league's first dynasty reached its third trophy. Thommy needed all three postseason wins without a bye, beginning from the No. 4 seed after a 7–6 regular season.

The postseason did not begin with evidence of invincibility. Birch had beaten Thommy by 58.76 points in Week 2; Tony had owned the best regular-season record. Thommy eliminated Tony in the semifinal and Birch in the final. That reversal is more powerful than calling the run inevitable. The older ESPN scores are unusually precise, but they do not provide a verified roster-level account of which individual starter created each margin.

seasons.title: Hogan’s Heroes Finish the Job
seasons.dek: An 11–2 juggernaut, a rematch with last year’s ghosts, and a championship held by 4.72 points.

sections.heading: A runner-up comes back with a statement
sections.text: Birch knew exactly what 4.96 points could cost. That was the margin by which Thommy had denied him the 2018 championship—and claimed a third straight ring. In 2019, Hogan's Heroes came back with a regular season built to change the ending. The opening week produced 169.32 against Tony. Five more victories followed. Birch was 6–0 before Koble finally stopped the run in Week 7, then Stover made it two straight defeats in Week 8. The finish, not the stumble, defined the record: five consecutive victories after those losses, 11–2 overall, and the No. 1 seed. It was a team that carried the best regular-season résumé into the bracket. The archived ESPN game record supports that arc; it does not give us a complete player-level season ledger from which to award a fantasy MVP.

sections.heading: The games that could have changed everything
sections.text: An 11–2 record looks comfortable in a trophy case. The games that created it were not always comfortable. Kuhl pushed Birch to 146.76–140.04 in Week 3, and Stew came within 8.40 points in Week 5. In Week 13, Birch needed nearly every point to beat Mitch 114.10–113.28—an escape by 0.82. Those narrow games mattered just as much to the 11–2 résumé as the spectacular routs. After the two midseason losses, Birch scored 147.94 against Stilly’s 75.00 and 153.74 against Tony’s 80.52, restoring the sense of a team capable of opening a huge gap. The championship run had both forms of strength: survive a week when the opponent is within a point, then put the next challenger away by seventy. The top seed was earned, not assumed.

sections.heading: Tony falls; Stew makes it a final
sections.text: The semifinal brought Tony back. Birch had already beaten him twice during the regular season, including the opening-week statement. The postseason version was closer, but Birch still produced 153.10 against Tony’s 131.52, a 21.58-point win. The final opponent was Stew, who had lost their regular-season meeting by 8.40. This one went down to the edge of the standings: Birch 114.14, Stew 109.42. The trophy was decided by 4.72 points. A year earlier, Birch had lost the championship by 4.96. Now, in a final even slightly tighter, he was the one who had done enough. The scoreboard does not establish which individual player swung the title; it establishes exactly how close the long-awaited breakthrough really was.

sections.heading: The difference between dominant and champion
sections.text: Some franchises build excellent regular seasons and never get to see them validated in the last game. Birch had seen both sides already—2018 finalist, 2019 runaway contender. The 11-win season would have been memorable regardless, but the 114.14–109.42 final changed its place in league history. Hogan’s Heroes were champions rather than another case of the highest seed being cut down. That is why the 0.82-point Week 13 win, the comeback after back-to-back losses and the 4.72-point title margin all belong in the same story. The recovered 2019 record has no complete individual playoff box score or trustworthy trade-to-lineup chain, so the account will not invent a roster savior. The team’s verified results are enough to explain how close the first Birch championship came to becoming another second-place finish. The finish also changed the balance of the league. For three seasons, every champion's line on the trophy had belonged to Thommy. Birch became the first manager to write a different name beneath that run. After losing the previous final to that same dynasty, Hogan's Heroes did not merely win a title; they made the history book belong to more than one franchise.

insideTheRun.heading: Redemption did not come with a comfortable lead
paragraphs: Birch's 11–2 season looked commanding from a distance. Up close, its championship depended on narrow escapes, including a Week 13 victory over Mitch by 0.82 points and a final against Stew that ended 114.14–109.42. The championship margin was only 4.72. A dominant regular-season record had earned Birch the advantageous position; it did not make the last matchup safe.

The opponent made that finish especially meaningful. A year after Birch had fallen 111.58–106.62 to Thommy in the 2018 final, the manager returned and won a title decided by almost the same margin. That is a documented arc of redemption rather than a claim about a mystery roster transaction. The 2019 archive preserves the matchup results and the move to half-PPR scoring, but not enough complete starter-level evidence to manufacture a specific game MVP.

seasons.title: The Sixth Seed Takes the Trophy
seasons.dek: A .500 regular season became a title run powered by Ryan Tannehill in the semifinal and David Johnson in the final.

sections.heading: Nothing about seven-and-seven said champion
sections.text: The last team into the 2020 Fellas playoffs walked out with the trophy. Koble had finished 7–7, claimed the sixth and final postseason berth and given the favorites little reason to fear the standings. December would make those standings look like an incomplete scouting report. Mitch went 9–4 and held the top seed; Birch also went 9–4 and took the other first-round bye. Koble’s own scores swung from a 143.34-point demolition of Mitch in Week 6 to a 50.58-point collapse against Tony in Week 10. He lost five of seven games across one midseason stretch, then did just enough late—beating Stilly in Week 12 and Kuhl in Week 14—to reach the bracket. This was not the league’s most consistent roster. Its great accomplishment before December was qualification. The archive identifies the sixth seed and later playoff scores, but the recovered first-round matchup does not supply a complete, responsibly quotable score.

sections.heading: Tannehill blows open the semifinal
sections.text: The regular season had offered no consensus superstar moment for this run. The semifinal supplied a name and an undeniable box score. Against Birch, the second seed, Koble scored 130.42 to Birch’s 82.82. Ryan Tannehill’s 37.02 points led Koble’s verified starting lineup. Derrick Henry supplied 24.20, David Johnson 17.80, and A.J. Brown 12.90. Those are archived player-level fantasy scores, not retrospective guesses about who looked important. The 47.60-point victory knocked out the other first-round bye team and reversed the expectation that a sixth seed should be overmatched by a nine-win contender. It also established something the earlier weekly ups and downs had obscured: Koble had enough scoring ceiling to separate from one of the bracket favorites when the season could end with a single defeat.

sections.heading: David Johnson takes the title-game stage
sections.text: The final against Mitch offered a rematch with the top seed and the league’s stronger regular-season résumé. Koble won 117.48–99.42, an 18.06-point margin. David Johnson was the championship-game scoring leader on the winning roster with 28.40 fantasy points. Jalen Hurts added 17.58 at quarterback; Miles Sanders contributed 15.40, Austin Ekeler 14.30 and the Baltimore defense 12.00. Those contributions explain the win better than any generic claim about getting hot at the right time. The lineup did not need one improbable hundred-point player; it needed a group of starters to put enough distance between a sixth seed and the No. 1 seed. The archived trade-evaluation dataset contains no verified Koble title-season trade that can be causally linked to this run. The lineup, not a fabricated transaction narrative, is the evidence.

sections.heading: What the upset means
sections.text: The sixth seed won the championship by defeating the bracket’s second seed and then its first. That is why 2020 remains a reference point whenever the Fellas argue about byes, regular-season dominance or whether a low seed is truly dangerous. The 7–7 season was not a prediction of what happened in Weeks 15 and 16. Tannehill’s 37.02 in the semifinal and David Johnson’s 28.40 in the championship are the individual peaks we can now name. Everything around them—the volatile season, the narrow path into the field and the two decisive wins—belongs to the verified record. Koble’s title is not a story about pretending the regular season did not matter; it is a story about how a team can survive that season and produce its best evidence after the bracket opens. When the next sixth seed enters a Fellas postseason, Koble's 2020 team is the uncomfortable precedent for whoever drew that matchup. The bye and the higher seed still matter; this championship doesn't disprove either. What it proves is narrower and harder to dismiss: once the bracket began, the lower seed produced the stronger scores in the games that awarded the trophy.

insideTheRun.heading: Two postseason heroes, two different jobs
paragraphs: Ryan Tannehill opened the decisive stretch by supplying 37.02 starter points in the 130.42–82.82 semifinal over Birch. Derrick Henry added 24.20. That 47.60-point semifinal margin ensured the sixth seed did not have to survive a last-drive nail-biter to reach the final. The title game against top-seeded Mitch required a different leading man: David Johnson posted 28.40, the highest verified total in Koble's winning lineup, as the championship finished 117.48–99.42.

Koble did not ride the identical performance twice. Tannehill led the semifinal scoring, while Jalen Hurts started at quarterback in the final and produced 17.58. Miles Sanders contributed 15.40 and Austin Ekeler 14.30 in the title game. The shift matters because it shows a balanced championship lineup rather than one mythical hot hand. What the record proves is the two-week contrast in actual starters, not why a particular quarterback was chosen or whether another lineup would have won.

seasons.title: Tony Wins the One That Counts
seasons.dek: Trades built the contenders; Mixon, Adams and the Tampa Bay defense delivered in a 4.30-point championship.

sections.heading: From four wins to a bye
sections.text: Tony went from 4–10 to champion in one season. The turnaround wasn't finished when he secured a 10–3 record, second place and a first-round bye: the last test would be a championship decided by just 4.30 points. There were obvious signs of the difference before the playoffs arrived. Tony scored 167.14 against Thommy in Week 6, then 151.46 against Kuhl in Week 7. Jonathan Taylor became a reliable foundation, producing 292.40 regular-season starter points across 13 credited starts. Matthew Stafford supplied 251.84 in 12, and Davante Adams added 211.40 in 12. Those are not vague descriptions of stars; they are the recorded points from the lineups Tony actually used during the completed regular season. Birch still finished 11–2 and took the top seed, so Tony entered December as a dangerous contender rather than the league’s automatic favorite.

sections.heading: The acquisitions weren't decorative
sections.text: The leap from four wins to ten had a documented roster-building trail—not merely a list of star names. An August 30 trade brought Tony Jonathan Taylor, A.J. Brown and Corey Davis, giving him the player who would lead his regular-season starting production. On October 5, Tony acquired Joe Mixon from Koble in a deal involving Zack Moss and James Robinson. On October 13 he traded Kareem Hunt for CeeDee Lamb; later that month a separate exchange brought Kyle Pitts Sr. The direct post-trade starter analysis is not a complete measure of value or keeper cost, and these moves cannot by themselves be declared wins. But their actual championship-week contribution is visible. Mixon, Lamb and Pitts were all in the starting lineup on the day Tony won the title. The trades matter because their acquired players were still on the field when the highest-stakes game was played.

sections.heading: A championship no one could relax through
sections.text: Tony’s semifinal against Stover ended 94.96–73.44. Jonathan Taylor provided 24.00 points, Stafford 15.46 and Adams 13.40; the margin was a comfortable 21.52. The final against Evans was not. Tony had beaten Evans twice during the regular season, including a 151.36–80.08 rout in Week 12, but the third matchup finished 138.28–133.98. Just 4.30 points separated a first trophy from another winter of what-ifs. Joe Mixon’s 29.50 led Tony’s starters, Davante Adams scored 28.40, and Tampa Bay’s defense supplied 19.00. Kyle Pitts added 13.20, CeeDee Lamb 8.40. In a championship decided by less than five points, the receipts establish the value of getting contributions from across the acquired and returning roster.

sections.heading: Who carried the season—and who closed it
sections.text: There is a useful distinction between season MVP and title-game MVP. Jonathan Taylor was Tony’s regular-season engine at 292.40 credited starter points; in the semifinal he again led the lineup. Joe Mixon was the leading scorer in the 138.28-point championship game. Adams was nearly as important on that last day, and the Tampa Bay defense created a 19-point margin of its own. It would be inaccurate to crown a single trade as the reason the trophy changed hands. It is accurate to say that Tony assembled a roster whose foundational running back got him to December, whose midseason acquisitions played in the final, and whose defense and receiving star helped preserve a four-point lead. After a 4–10 year, 2021 delivered not just contention but the finish. For Tony, the last margin was the whole difference between a remarkable turnaround and a season remembered chiefly for falling short. That is why the acquisition trail, Taylor's long regular-season production and Mixon's last-week points belong in one account. The roster was built across months; the title came down to 4.30 points. Both timelines matter.

insideTheRun.heading: The margin was smaller than a single defensive play
paragraphs: Tony defeated Evans 138.28–133.98, just 4.30 points apart. Joe Mixon's 29.50 and Davante Adams's 28.40 were the headline championship performances, together accounting for 57.90 of Tony's total. But the Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense supplied 19.00, and Alexander Mattison added 14.50. In a final this close, it would be misleading to reduce the outcome to one star: there were several different ways those starting-lineup points mattered.

The semifinal tells a different story. Jonathan Taylor led Tony with 24.00 in the 94.96–73.44 victory over Stover; his championship contribution was 11.80. Taylor was essential to the season-long ascent, while Mixon and Adams supplied the title-game fireworks. That is why the verified acquisition trail matters: it connects the managers' roster-building decisions to the players who actually appeared on the championship scoresheet, rather than assigning retroactive credit to every trade.

editorialVerdicts.label: Regular-season engine

seasons.title: Stover Settles the Score
seasons.dek: Mahomes and a four-star regular-season core earned the bye; a 51.06-point final win ended Stew’s dream season.

sections.heading: Four pillars, one unfinished piece of business
sections.text: Eleven wins had not bought Stover a title in 2021. The next year, nine wins would be enough to get him back into position—and a strange, interrupted NFL Week 17 would leave the Fellas with a championship result that deserved both a trophy and careful reporting. Stew went 11–3 and claimed the No. 1 seed. Stover finished 9–5, enough for second place and a first-round bye. But the lineup evidence explains why the challenger was dangerous: Patrick Mahomes supplied 316.40 regular-season starter points in 13 starts, Tyreek Hill 246.00, Derrick Henry 234.06 and Travis Kelce 217.90. The four combined for more than a thousand credited starting fantasy points before the postseason. Those are the players who built the runway to December. This was a roster with both a stable quarterback and elite options at multiple positions, not a late-season collection built around one lucky week.

sections.heading: The favorite had already beaten him
sections.text: The path back to that final included an opponent who had already shown Stover exactly how far he had to climb. In Week 2, Stew beat Stover 159.72–119.60. It was the kind of loss that can establish an early hierarchy, and the eventual standings still favored Stew. Stover did get an answer in Week 11, scoring 137.62 in a 27.82-point victory over the same opponent. There were delicate moments elsewhere: he beat Tony 132.68–129.50 in Week 5, a margin of just 3.18, and Birch 119.82–113.92 in Week 7. Those wins helped preserve the record needed for the bye. A December contender is rarely built only from spectacular scoring totals. Sometimes the three-point September win is the difference between playing an extra elimination game and resting as a top-two seed.

sections.heading: The semifinal, the final, and the decisive players
sections.text: Kuhl awaited in the semifinal. Stover won 112.56–87.68, with Mahomes contributing 23.76 points, Devin Singletary 19.50, Henry 18.60 and Kelce 15.30. The championship was the showdown the standings had suggested: No. 1 Stew against No. 2 Stover. The archived league scoreboard finished Stover 99.22, Stew 48.16, but this final needs an unusual historical qualifier: the Buffalo–Cincinnati NFL Week 17 game was canceled, affecting fantasy scoring. The numbers here are the verified recorded Fellas totals, not evidence of how the game would have ended had every NFL matchup been completed. Mahomes again led the winning lineup, this time with 25.02. DJ Moore added 21.70 and the New York Giants defense delivered 16.00. Hill contributed 13.70. The championship-game lineup was not an identical mirror of the regular-season top scorers, and that is the point: the core earned the opportunity, while the actual Week 17 starters won it by 51.06 points.

sections.heading: Gurt gets its place on the trophy
sections.text: The decisive final changed the meaning of the previous year’s near miss. A manager who had already put together an 11-win season without a title now had the outcome the league remembers. Stover did not need the best regular-season record in 2022; he needed to survive close games, reach the bye and beat Kuhl before the unusually disrupted Week 17 championship. The verified league record awards him the victory over Stew. Mahomes is the clearest individual through-line: the leading regular-season starter and the leading championship-week scorer. Moore’s 21.70 and the Giants defense’s 16.00 deserve their own place in the title-game account because they were confirmed points, not a convenient post hoc story. The archived trade dataset does not establish a defining 2022 Stover acquisition, so this championship is best told through the lineup core and the final scoreboard. There is an important distinction in the final-week evidence. The archived championship was played under the unusual Week 17 circumstances, and the official league result—not a reconstruction of what unplayed football might have produced—determines the title. Stover still had to earn the berth, win the semifinal and finish ahead on the recorded scoreboard. That is the history the trophy preserves.

insideTheRun.heading: A championship score with a necessary asterisk
paragraphs: Stover's semifinal over Kuhl was a clean 112.56–87.68 win, paced by Patrick Mahomes at 23.76, Devin Singletary at 19.50 and Derrick Henry at 18.60. In the final against Stew, Mahomes again led the starting lineup at 25.02. DJ Moore delivered 21.70 and the New York Giants defense contributed 16.00, helping produce the archived 99.22–48.16 result.

That final cannot be described responsibly as an ordinary uninterrupted blowout. The canceled Buffalo–Cincinnati game in NFL Week 17 affected the fantasy championship environment, and the archive records the resulting score rather than an alternate outcome that nobody can verify. Stover is the official champion; Mahomes, Moore and the Giants are documented contributors to his lineup. The fairest journalism keeps both statements visible: honor the result without pretending the week played out normally.

seasons.title: From 0–4 to Fellas Champion
seasons.dek: A late trade, an eight-win turnaround and the defensive points that helped Stilly finish the impossible run.

sections.heading: Four weeks in, no wins and no obvious answers
sections.text: Four weeks. Four losses. Not a single win—and, by December, a Fellas championship. In September 2023, Stilly was losing to Mitch, Stew, Tony and Stover in succession, with no reason yet to imagine the league's next trophy ending in his hands. After four weeks, Stilly was 0–4, looking up at a league that seemed to be sorting contenders without him. The first win came against Evans in Week 5, 127.36–98.72, but the recovery still had fragile moments. In Week 8 he edged Thommy 120.36–117.58, a 2.78-point result that mattered greatly in an eventual 8–6 record. Josh Allen became the quarterback foundation across the regular season, contributing 306.28 credited starter points in 13 starts. Michael Pittman Jr. added 155.20 and Rachaad White 127.20. Those are the weekly starters who helped turn a lost opening month into a competitive season.

sections.heading: The Kupp trade becomes part of the answer
sections.text: The comeback did not happen by wishful thinking alone. On October 26, Stilly sent Cooper Kupp to Tony and received Mike Evans and Derrick Henry. The move was not just a transaction people would remember afterward; the two incoming players actually mattered in the games that decided the season. Stilly won his final four regular-season contests, including 173.86–99.58 over Tony in Week 12 and 159.66–89.10 over Stover in Week 13. The 0–4 team finished 8–6, fourth in the regular-season standings and forced to play the opening playoff round. Against Birch, Stilly won 146.36–105.06. Against Tony in the semifinal, the trade’s relevance became measurable: Evans scored 24.10 and Henry 20.88, a combined 44.98 of Stilly’s 141.66 points in a 141.66–108.58 victory over the same manager who had dealt them to him.

sections.heading: The final obstacle had beaten him twice
sections.text: Mitch was waiting in the championship. He had beaten Stilly in Week 1 and again in Week 10, so the final required another reversal of the regular-season script. Stilly’s championship lineup did not simply repeat its semifinal formula. Josh Allen led with 19.16, the Buffalo Bills defense supplied 18.00, David Njoku added 15.40, Aaron Jones 13.50 and David Montgomery 12.50. The famous October acquisitions were still in the starting lineup—Evans scored 8.50 and Henry 4.20—but the title was earned by the full group, including a defense that nearly matched the quarterback. The final finished Stilly 104.96, Mitch 90.18. The 14.78-point margin was enough to end a season that, four weeks in, had contained no wins at all.

sections.heading: What actually changed the story
sections.text: It is easy to say the Kupp trade won a championship. The evidence supports a more interesting and more precise conclusion. Evans and Henry were decisive semifinal contributors and represented an observable way the roster changed; Allen was the steady regular-season engine and the title game’s top scorer; Buffalo’s defense and Njoku gave the final its crucial supporting production. The late regular-season winning streak supplied the playoff berth, and three consecutive playoff victories—over Birch, Tony and Mitch—supplied the ring. In the same postseason Stilly beat the regular-season leader and the opponent who had beaten him twice. That is why 2023 deserves more than a generic comeback label: it connects the transaction receipt, specific starters and scoreboard reversals into one verified championship run. The most revealing rematch was against Tony: the manager who received Kupp became the semifinal opponent facing the players sent the other way. But the final refused to reduce itself to that transaction. Stilly needed Allen, Njoku and Buffalo's defense to finish against Mitch. The comeback is remembered for the trade; the record shows a championship won in different ways on successive Sundays.

insideTheRun.heading: The blockbuster got him there; the supporting cast finished it
paragraphs: The October 26 trade sending Cooper Kupp to Tony for Mike Evans and Derrick Henry becomes vivid in the semifinal box score. Evans produced 24.10 and Henry 20.88 in the 141.66–108.58 victory; together, the two incoming players supplied 44.98 starter points. Josh Allen added 24.98. That trio helps explain how a team that began 0–4 arrived in a championship game instead of watching December from the sidelines.

The title game required another kind of performance. Against Mitch, Allen delivered 19.16, but the Buffalo Bills defense recorded 18.00 and David Njoku supplied 15.40 as Stilly won 104.96–90.18. Evans had 8.50 and Henry 4.20 in the final. Calling the trade the sole reason for the trophy would erase the players who closed the season. Calling it irrelevant would erase the verified semifinal that made the final possible. The full truth makes a better story.

seasons.title: The Fourth Ring, Six Years Later
seasons.dek: A 2.30-point semifinal escape, a consequential Tee Higgins trade and a 205.30-point championship eruption.

sections.heading: A dynasty trying to prove it still existed
sections.text: One week, Thommy survived by 2.30 points. The next, he scored 205.30 to win his fourth Fellas championship. That was the unlikely ending waiting for a manager whose first three rings had come consecutively from 2016 through 2018—and whose next six seasons had brought no new engraving. Six straight wins to open the season revived the conversation. The regular-season core was built around Derrick Henry and Bijan Robinson: Henry produced 248.70 credited starter points in 13 starts and Robinson added 220.30 in 13. A 152.02–79.78 win over Tony in Week 6 showed the ceiling. Four defeats over the final eight regular-season weeks kept the campaign from feeling inevitable, but Thommy finished 9–5, earned the No. 2 seed and secured a bye. The original champion had his route back; the bracket still demanded that he finish it.

sections.heading: The trade that becomes visible in the final
sections.text: The regular-season foundation was in place, but a September transaction would become visible on the biggest scoreboard of all. On September 24, Thommy received Christian McCaffrey, Diontae Johnson and Tee Higgins from Stilly, who got Terry McLaurin, De’Von Achane and Tank Dell. The receipt proves the players changed teams; it does not settle who won the trade across a full season. Yet the championship evidence supplies one unusually clear piece of its legacy. Higgins remained on Thommy’s roster and scored 34.60 fantasy points in the title game. Another October transaction brought Jordan Love, who started that final and scored 14.00. A separate October 17 trade brought Travis Kelce, who supplied 5.50 points in the razor-thin semifinal and 18.40 in the championship lineup. Those moves matter here not because a trade chart says they were clever but because specific incoming players contributed verifiable points to the championship lineup. The season-long foundation still came from Henry and Robinson, which makes the acquired pieces complements rather than a convenient explanation for everything.

sections.heading: Two points from elimination, then an avalanche
sections.text: JMid had beaten Thommy 107.24–103.80 in Week 7 and led the league in regular-season scoring. Their semifinal rematch was even tighter: Thommy 123.38, JMid 121.08. A margin of 2.30 was all that preserved the fourth-ring chance. Jameson Williams led Thommy’s starters with 24.50, Robinson added 23.30 and Henry 20.90. The final was against Stilly, the defending champion. This time the drama was not about a narrow edge. Thommy scored 205.30 to Stilly’s 114.88. Higgins led all Thommy starters with 34.60; DeVonta Smith delivered 28.00, Adam Thielen 26.50, Henry 23.50, Robinson 22.30 and Williams 22.00. The winning margin was 90.42, a stunning transformation from a semifinal survived by fewer than three points.

sections.heading: An old champion, a new kind of title
sections.text: The significance of Thommy’s fourth ring is not only that he extended the league lead. The early dynasty had been built in a different era and a different scoring environment. This title came six seasons after the third, on a roster anchored by Henry and Robinson and supplemented by moves that could be traced directly into the decisive lineup. Higgins’ 34.60 makes him the championship-game scoring MVP by the recorded starter totals; Williams’ 24.50 helped keep the season alive one round earlier. If either the 2.30-point semifinal result or the final’s outburst is missing from the account, the story loses its essential contrast. One week the dynasty hung by a thread. The next it won by ninety. That is the fourth ring’s real signature. The fourth title also changed how every earlier Thommy championship would be remembered. The first three came consecutively, under the older league format; this one survived a six-season gap, a 2.30-point escape and a wildly different championship week. The final was emphatic, but the semifinal is what gave the eruption its weight. Without the escape, there is no fourth engraving.

insideTheRun.heading: The moment before the avalanche
paragraphs: Before Thommy's 205.30-point championship masterpiece, the entire season balanced on 2.30 points. JMid lost the semifinal 123.38–121.08. Jameson Williams led Thommy's starters at 24.50, with Bijan Robinson at 23.30 and Derrick Henry at 20.90. No fourth ring happens without that narrow result. The final score can make the title feel inevitable in hindsight, but the preceding playoff game proves it was anything but.

Then came a title-game lineup with five players scoring at least 22 points: Tee Higgins 34.60, DeVonta Smith 28.00, Adam Thielen 26.50, Derrick Henry 23.50 and Bijan Robinson 22.30. Higgins had arrived in the September trade involving Stilly, so the connection between transaction and championship points is documented. Thommy beat Stilly 205.30–114.88, a 90.42-point final margin. The correct headline is not simply dominance: it is two points from going home, followed by one of the league's most emphatic title performances.

seasons.title: Scott’s Fast Track to the Trophy
seasons.dek: A second-year leap, a 0.98-point September escape, and a final carried by Bijan Robinson and Brock Purdy.

sections.heading: The second-year manager against an established order
sections.text: Scott's first Fellas season ended 5–9. His second ended with a trophy—and with four-time champion Thommy on the wrong side of a 156.32–86.00 final. The rise began with an 8–6 regular season that earned a playoff bye, not with a single December miracle. That would have been a remarkable improvement even without the trophy. Mitch went 13–1 and entered December as the regular season’s defining powerhouse; Thommy had four championships. Scott was not the most obvious name to put above either of them. But his roster had earned attention. Bijan Robinson produced 239.30 credited regular-season starter points across 13 starts, James Cook III 221.00, George Pickens 206.90 and Trey McBride 188.20. Those four were the regular-season backbone. The 2025 story is not one miracle player appearing in the final; it begins with a balanced collection that made a new contender possible.

sections.heading: The games that kept the path open
sections.text: Long before the two postseason blowouts, Scott needed a September win measured in hundredths. He opened with three straight victories, including a Week 3 finish against Stover that ended 113.52–112.54, a win by just 0.98. Over a full season, that sort of game can decide who reaches a bye and who travels the hard side of the bracket. There were reminders of the gap to the league’s strongest regular-season team: Mitch beat Scott 180.86–136.06 in Week 7. But there were also signs of Scott’s own ceiling. He scored 154.76 in a Week 6 win over Stew, then 155.10 against JMid’s 53.72 in Week 11. Scott finished 8–6 rather than 13–1, yet he carried a first-round bye and enough high-scoring weeks to threaten any opponent. The available title-season trade ledger does not establish a decisive Scott acquisition; the story’s foundation is the observed starting lineup.

sections.heading: First the semifinal; then the four-time champion
sections.text: Scott met Birch in the semifinal and won 141.88–70.40, a 71.48-point margin. Robinson scored 27.30, Cook 26.90 and Pickens 22.50; all three had already been major regular-season contributors. Thommy awaited in the final, carrying four titles and a 165.50–130.74 regular-season win over Scott from Week 4. The championship reversed that precedent emphatically. Scott scored 156.32 to Thommy’s 86.00. Robinson led the winners with 38.40 and Brock Purdy scored 36.92—75.32 points from two starters in a game won by 70.32. The New York Giants defense added 20.00, Christian Watson 19.80 and McBride 18.60. That is a title-game MVP partnership with receipts, not a claim based on reputation.

sections.heading: The trophy belongs to the player who finishes
sections.text: The two postseason wins came by 71.48 and 70.32 points, a combined 141.80-point advantage. It is a striking ending for a manager who had finished 5–9 in his first season and survived a September game by less than a point. Robinson is the clearest through-line: Scott’s leading regular-season starter, the semifinal’s top scorer and the championship’s leading scorer. Cook and Pickens helped win the semifinal; Purdy supplied the championship-week explosion alongside Robinson. Scott did not have to finish ahead of Mitch in the regular-season standings or outlast Thommy’s dynasty over a decade. He had to get into the bracket, make the most of his bye and outscore two opponents when it mattered. By Week 17, the second-year newcomer had changed the Fellas’ hierarchy. The final offered the sharpest possible handoff: Scott defeated Thommy, the four-time champion whose name had defined so much of the league's first decade. There was no need to invent a decade-long rivalry to make the moment significant. The verified result was enough. In his second season, Scott arrived in the same championship ledger as the league's oldest powers—and did it decisively.

insideTheRun.heading: A second-year champion who left no doubt in December
paragraphs: The 113.52–112.54 Week 3 win over Stover is easy to forget beside the trophy photographs. It should not be: a 0.98-point result helped shape an 8–6 season that ultimately earned Scott a playoff bye. When the postseason came, the second-year manager changed from survivor to runaway winner. Bijan Robinson recorded 27.30 and James Cook III 26.90 in the 141.88–70.40 semifinal against Birch, with George Pickens adding 22.50.

The championship against four-time winner Thommy brought an even louder answer. Robinson scored 38.40, Brock Purdy 36.92 and the New York Giants defense 20.00 as Scott won 156.32–86.00. Robinson was the postseason constant, but Purdy's final-week contribution is what distinguishes the title-game version of the team from its semifinal version. Scott's two playoff wins totaled a 141.80-point margin; what began as a second-year breakthrough ended as an emphatic arrival.
